questions.question: How do MySQL and PostgreSQL compare for Java backend developers, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.title: MySQL vs PostgreSQL for Java Developers
questions.direct_answer: MySQL and PostgreSQL are both excellent relational databases fully supported by Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. PostgreSQL leads on SQL standards compliance, advanced data types (JSONB, arrays, ranges), window functions, and extensibility. MySQL leads on read replication ease, widespread hosting support, and marginally simpler operational overhead for standard CRUD workloads. The choice depends on query complexity, cloud environment, and team familiarity.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests breadth of database knowledge and ability to make pragmatic technology choices. Interviewers want to hear trade-off reasoning, not just a preference. Shows whether the candidate has worked with both databases in production Java contexts.

sections.title: Two Great Databases — Different Sweet Spots
sections.content: MySQL and PostgreSQL are both mature, open-source relational databases with full ACID compliance and excellent Spring Boot/JPA/Hibernate support. Their differences matter most at the edges: complex queries, advanced data types, replication architecture, and strict SQL standards compliance. For a standard Spring Boot CRUD application, both work equally well and switching between them requires only a dependency change and dialect update in Spring Boot.

sections.content:
### MySQL vs PostgreSQL — Java Developer Perspective

| Feature | MySQL 8.0 | PostgreSQL 16 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQL Standards Compliance | ⚠️ Good, some deviations | ✅ Excellent, most compliant |
| JSON Support | ⚠️ JSON (no indexing on paths) | ✅ JSONB (indexed, operators) |
| Window Functions | ✅ Supported (8.0+) | ✅ Supported, more complete |
| CTEs (WITH clause) | ✅ Supported (8.0+) | ✅ Supported, WITH RECURSIVE |
| Full-Text Search | ⚠️ Basic built-in | ✅ Advanced with tsvector/tsquery |
| Read Replication | ✅ Simple binlog replication | ⚠️ More complex WAL streaming |
| Horizontal Sharding | ⚠️ Needs Vitess/ProxySQL | ⚠️ Needs Citus extension |
| Spring Boot Dialect | ✅ MySQLDialect | ✅ PostgreSQLDialect |
| Cloud Managed Options | ✅ RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL | ✅ RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Supabase |
| Schema Migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) | ✅ Full support | ✅ Full support |
| Array / Range Types | ❌ Not supported | ✅ Native array, range, hstore |
| Transactional DDL | ❌ DDL auto-commits | ✅ DDL in transactions (rollback on fail) |
| Default Port | 3306 | 5432 |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PostgreSQL JSONB with GIN index vs MySQL JSON** — PostgreSQL allows `WHERE data @> '{"status": "active"}'` to use a GIN index; MySQL JSON queries have more limited index support and require generated column indexes for performance
- **MySQL Repeatable Read uses gap locks; PostgreSQL uses MVCC** — gap locks in MySQL under the default isolation level cause more deadlocks in concurrent insert workloads; PostgreSQL's MVCC approach avoids them
- **PostgreSQL: arrays, ranges, enums as native types** — MySQL requires workaround tables or JSON for the same data; PostgreSQL's richer type system reduces schema complexity for certain domains
- **Hibernate dialect is the only Spring Boot change** — `org.hibernate.dialect.MySQLDialect` vs `PostgreSQLDialect`; JPA queries, `@Transactional`, and Spring Data repositories behave identically on both
- **Aurora MySQL and RDS MySQL are more mature managed offerings** — for teams deploying on AWS who need managed replication and failover, MySQL's managed ecosystem is broader; Aurora PostgreSQL has caught up but MySQL is more commonly chosen for simpler operational reasons

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
For a standard Spring Boot CRUD application, MySQL and PostgreSQL are largely interchangeable at the surface — you swap the JDBC driver and Hibernate dialect and most applications work unchanged. The differences emerge at the edges.

**Where PostgreSQL has a clear advantage**
- PostgreSQL's type system is richer — JSONB with GIN indexing allows complex JSON queries at near-relational speed, whereas MySQL's JSON support has more limited indexing options; arrays and range types are native in PostgreSQL, requiring workarounds in MySQL
- PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevents phantom reads via MVCC without gap locks — MySQL's Repeatable Read uses gap locks under Repeatable Read, which causes more deadlocks in insert-heavy workloads
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL shows actual vs estimated rows, actual time, and buffer hits; MySQL 8.0 added EXPLAIN ANALYZE but PostgreSQL's planner output is generally more detailed

**Where MySQL has a clear advantage**
- MySQL's ecosystem and tooling are more widely deployed — RDS, Aurora, and managed MySQL are ubiquitous; many teams have more operational experience with MySQL, which matters more than feature differences for standard workloads
- MySQL's replication is simpler to configure for basic primary-replica setups; Aurora MySQL with failover is more mature than Aurora PostgreSQL in some managed environments
- Full-text search is easier to enable on MySQL InnoDB tables for basic search needs, though Elasticsearch or PostgreSQL's full-text capabilities often replace it at scale

**For Spring Boot specifically**
- Hibernate works identically on both — dialect selection is the only difference in `application.properties`; JPA queries, `@Transactional`, and Spring Data repositories behave the same
- MySQL autocommit defaults mean each statement outside an explicit transaction is committed immediately; ensure `@Transactional` is applied wherever multiple operations must be atomic

questions.question: What are window functions in PostgreSQL? Explain RANK, ROW_NUMBER, and LEAD/LAG with examples.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Window Functions — RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG/LEAD
questions.direct_answer: Window functions perform calculations across related rows without grouping them away. RANK/DENSE_RANK compute position within a partition. ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequential numbers. LAG/LEAD access previous/next row values without a self-join.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can solve ranking and trend analysis problems without complex subqueries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using RANK vs ROW_NUMBER incorrectly — RANK leaves gaps for ties, ROW_NUMBER never does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER with tie examples and explain the OVER clause components

sections.content: Window functions are PostgreSQL's answer to the 'how do I compute per-row rankings or trend data without losing rows via GROUP BY?' question. The OVER clause defines the window: which rows participate (PARTITION BY) and in what order (ORDER BY).

-- Sample data:
-- employees: id, dept, name, salary

-- RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER (shows tie behavior)
SELECT
    name, dept, salary,
    RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num
FROM employees;

-- For two employees in ENG with salary=95000:
-- name     | dept | salary | rank | dense_rank | row_num
-- Alice    | ENG  | 95000  |  1   |     1      |   1
-- Bob      | ENG  | 95000  |  1   |     1      |   2  ← row_num always unique
-- Charlie  | ENG  | 80000  |  3   |     2      |   3  ← rank skips to 3, dense_rank=2

-- LAG/LEAD: access adjacent rows (no self-join needed)
SELECT
    month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month)  AS prev_month_revenue,
    LEAD(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next_month_revenue,
    revenue - LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS month_over_month_delta
FROM monthly_sales
ORDER BY month;

-- Find top-1 earner per department (use ROW_NUMBER for unique top-1)
SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, dept, salary,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
    FROM employees
) t
WHERE rn = 1;

- **ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on ties** — `RANK` skips numbers after ties (1,1,3); `DENSE_RANK` does not (1,1,2); `ROW_NUMBER` assigns arbitrary unique integers; choose based on whether gaps in ranking matter to the use case
- **ROW_NUMBER deduplication** — `PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY created_at DESC` + outer `WHERE rn = 1` keeps the latest row per group; replaces correlated subqueries and self-joins
- **Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY** — cannot filter on window results in WHERE; wrap in a CTE or subquery, then apply the filter in the outer query
- **LAG/LEAD eliminate self-joins for row comparison** — `amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` computes period-over-period change in one pass; a self-join on date equality does the same with more complexity
- **PARTITION BY is optional** — omitting it applies the function globally across all rows; adding it scopes the calculation to each partition independently

Window functions perform calculations across related rows without collapsing them — unlike GROUP BY which gives you one row per group, window functions annotate every row with a computed value while keeping all rows visible.

**ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK — the tie question**
- `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns unique sequential integers regardless of ties — so two employees with the same salary get 1 and 2 arbitrarily
- `RANK()` assigns the same number to ties but skips after them (1, 1, 3) — so the next-highest salary is rank 3, not rank 2
- `DENSE_RANK()` assigns the same number to ties and doesn't skip (1, 1, 2) — which means the next-highest salary is always one step above the tied group; use this when gaps in ranking would be confusing to users

**PARTITION BY and ORDER BY — the two control levers**
- `PARTITION BY` divides rows into groups for the window function to operate within — `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC)` ranks each employee within their department, not globally
- Without PARTITION BY, the function operates across the entire result set; combining both gives you group-scoped rankings without GROUP BY

**Deduplication with ROW_NUMBER**
- The most common production use: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` assigns rank 1 to each user's latest record — wrap it in a CTE or subquery and filter `WHERE rn = 1` to keep only the latest row per user without a correlated subquery or self-join

**LAG and LEAD for row-to-row comparisons**
- `LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` returns the previous row's value — `amount - LAG(amount)` computes month-over-month change in one pass, eliminating a self-join on date columns
- `SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` computes a running total without any subquery

Window functions execute after WHERE and GROUP BY but before ORDER BY — filter on window function results by wrapping the query in a CTE or subquery.

questions.question: How do you read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output in PostgreSQL? How do you optimize a slow query?
questions.title: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE — PostgreSQL Query Optimization
questions.direct_answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows actual vs estimated rows, execution time, and the chosen plan nodes. Look for Seq Scan on large tables (needs index), high cost nodes, and large row estimate mismatches (stale statistics). Use indexes, rewrite subqueries, or update statistics to fix.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to diagnose and fix slow queries using PostgreSQL's built-in tools
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding an index without understanding why the planner chose a Seq Scan — sometimes Seq Scan is the right choice for small tables or low-selectivity queries
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the cost model (random_page_cost, seq_page_cost) and why VACUUM ANALYZE is needed for accurate estimates

sections.content: EXPLAIN shows the query plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows actual statistics. Always use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in production for full diagnostic information including cache hit/miss data.

-- Full diagnostic EXPLAIN:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'PENDING'
  AND o.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;

-- Sample output (annotated):
-- HashAggregate  (cost=1250..1290 rows=100 width=40)
--               (actual time=45.2..48.1 rows=87 loops=1)
--   ->  Hash Join  (cost=450..1200 rows=1000 width=20)
--                 (actual time=12.3..43.5 rows=1543 loops=1)
--         ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0..900 rows=5000 width=8)
--             ↑ RED FLAG! Scanning all orders
--             Filter: (status='PENDING' AND created_at > ...)
--             Rows Removed by Filter: 48457     ← 90% waste!
--             (actual time=0.1..30.2 rows=5000 loops=1)
--         ->  Hash on users  (cost=200..200 rows=1000 width=40)
-- Planning Time: 0.5ms
-- Execution Time: 48.9ms

-- FIX: Composite index on filter columns
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status_created
    ON orders (status, created_at DESC)
    WHERE status = 'PENDING';  -- partial index: only pending orders!

-- After index:
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_status_created on orders
--   (cost=0.44..45 rows=1543 width=8)
--   (actual time=0.08..2.1 rows=1543 loops=1)
-- Execution Time: 4.2ms  (90% faster!)

sections.title: Reading Node Types and Identifying Performance Bottlenecks
sections.content:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE output is a tree of execution nodes. Each node type tells you what the database is doing; the actual vs estimated row counts tell you whether the planner made good predictions.

**Sequential Scan (Seq Scan)** reads the entire table row by row. This is efficient for small tables or when you're selecting a large percentage of rows (>10-20%). It becomes a performance killer on large tables when only a few rows match — that's the signal to add an index.

**Index Scan vs Index Only Scan.** An Index Scan reads the index to find matching row pointers, then fetches the actual rows from the table (a heap fetch). An Index Only Scan reads everything from the index without touching the table — possible only when all columns in the SELECT and WHERE are covered by the index. Index Only Scans show `Heap Fetches: 0` when the visibility map is up-to-date (run `VACUUM` if heap fetches are high).

**Nested Loop vs Hash Join vs Merge Join.** Nested Loop is efficient when the inner table is small or has a fast index lookup. Hash Join builds a hash table from one input and probes it with the other — efficient for medium-to-large joins without indexes. Merge Join sorts both inputs and merges them — efficient when both inputs are already sorted (e.g., by an index).

```
-- Example EXPLAIN ANALYZE output with annotations
Hash Join  (cost=45.00..150.00 rows=200 width=40) (actual time=1.2..5.8 rows=180 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.user_id = u.id)
  -> Seq Scan on orders o  (actual time=0.01..3.2 rows=5000 loops=1)
       Filter: (status = 'PENDING')          -- rows removed by filter: 45000
  -> Hash  (actual time=0.8..0.8 rows=100 loops=1)
       -> Index Scan on users u  (actual time=0.02..0.5 rows=100 loops=1)
```

**The "rows removed by filter" line is your optimization signal.** If a Seq Scan shows `actual rows=5000` but `rows removed by filter: 45000`, the database read 50,000 rows to return 5,000 — an index on the filter column would eliminate 90% of the I/O. Compare estimated `rows` with actual `rows` — if they differ by more than 10x, run `ANALYZE tablename` to update planner statistics.

- **`EXPLAIN` vs `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`** — EXPLAIN shows planner estimates; ANALYZE executes and shows actual rows and time; always use ANALYZE in development to make decisions on real execution, not predictions
- **Seq Scan = no index used** — filter column lacks an index, or planner chose a scan because statistics are stale; run `ANALYZE tablename` to refresh, then re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE
- **`Index Only Scan` is the ideal** — all selected columns are in the index; no heap pages are read; the highest-performance plan for read-heavy queries
- **Large estimate vs actual rows gap signals stale statistics** — `rows=100` vs `actual rows=50000` means the planner chose wrong; `ANALYZE` updates the statistics the optimizer uses for cost estimation
- **`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` reveals cache vs disk** — `shared hit` = buffer cache; `blocks read` = disk; a cache-bound query is fast; a disk-bound query benefits from larger `shared_buffers` or a covering index

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL shows exactly how a query executes — actual row counts, actual execution times, and the plan nodes chosen — not estimates. The difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE matters: EXPLAIN predicts, ANALYZE proves.

**Reading the plan output**
- `Seq Scan` on a large table means PostgreSQL read every row — the most urgent signal; look for a missing index on the filter column, or stale statistics causing the planner to underestimate cardinality
- `Index Scan` means a B-tree was traversed and heap rows were fetched by rowid; `Index Only Scan` means all needed columns were in the index, so the heap was never read — the ideal for read queries
- `Bitmap Heap Scan` sits between the two: PostgreSQL collects matching rowids from the index, sorts them by physical location, then reads heap pages in order — more efficient than Index Scan for high-selectivity range queries

**Estimations vs actuals**
- The `rows=X` estimate comes from table statistics; when `actual rows=50000` but `estimated rows=100`, the planner chose the wrong plan based on stale statistics — run `ANALYZE tablename` to update them
- High discrepancy in row estimates is the most common root cause of suboptimal plan selection; always look for it before adding an index

**BUFFERS — cache vs disk**
- `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` adds `shared hit=N` (read from PostgreSQL buffer cache) and `blocks read=N` (disk I/O) — a query with 0 disk reads is cache-bound; the same query hitting disk for 50,000 blocks is roughly 100x slower
- This tells you whether the fix is a plan change or simply ensuring the working set fits in `shared_buffers`

Use `pg_stat_statements` to find the true slowest queries by total execution time across all sessions — not just the queries you suspect. Queries that run fast but are called millions of times are often the largest contributors to total database load.

questions.question: What types of indexes does PostgreSQL support? When do you use each?
questions.title: PostgreSQL Index Types — B-Tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Hash
questions.direct_answer: B-Tree is the default for equality and range queries. GIN is for full-text search and JSONB queries. GiST handles geometric and range types. BRIN is extremely compact for naturally ordered large tables. Hash is fast for equality only.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know more than just 'add an index' — correct index type for the access pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using B-Tree for JSONB attribute queries (requires GIN) or for full-text search
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain partial indexes, covering indexes (INCLUDE), and when to use expression indexes

sections.content: Index type selection is about matching the index data structure to the access pattern. B-Tree's sorted structure handles range queries perfectly. GIN's inverted index handles multi-value containment efficiently. Wrong index type = index that exists but is never used.

| Index Type | Best For | Operators Supported | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| B-Tree (default) | Equality, ranges, ORDER BY | =, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN | Covers 90% of use cases |
| GIN | JSONB, arrays, full-text search | @>, <@, @@, @@ | Large index size, slow writes |
| GiST | Geometry, ranges, nearest-neighbor | &&, <<, >>, @> | Used by PostGIS |
| BRIN | Very large tables, sequential data | =, < ,> (approx) | Tiny size, great for time series |
| Hash | Equality only, no ranges | = | Rarely better than B-Tree |

**Practical examples:**
```sql
-- B-Tree (default): user lookups, date ranges
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created
    ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

-- GIN: JSONB attribute queries
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs
    ON products USING GIN (attributes);
-- Enables: WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'

-- GIN: Full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_search
    ON articles USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || body));
-- Enables: WHERE to_tsvector(...) @@ to_tsquery('postgresql')

-- BRIN: IoT sensor data (ordered by time)
CREATE INDEX idx_sensor_time
    ON sensor_readings USING BRIN (recorded_at);
-- 1000x smaller than B-Tree, perfect for time series

-- Partial index: only active users
CREATE INDEX idx_active_users_email
    ON users (email)
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Covering index (INCLUDE): eliminates heap fetch
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering
    ON orders (user_id)
    INCLUDE (status, total_amount, created_at);
-- Query: SELECT status, total_amount FROM orders WHERE user_id=42
-- → Index Only Scan (never touches the table!)

-- Expression index: case-insensitive lookup
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower
    ON users (LOWER(email));
-- WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com'
```

- **GIN for JSONB containment and full-text search** — `@>` (contains) and `@@` (text search) operators use GIN; B-tree cannot index multi-value or inverted lookup patterns
- **GiST for geometric and range types** — overlap, containment, and nearest-neighbor queries on geometry and range columns; the only index type that handles spatial operators
- **Composite B-tree left-prefix rule** — `(a, b)` cannot serve `WHERE b = ?` alone; the leading column must be in the filter
- **Partial index reduces index size and maintenance cost** — `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'` indexes only active rows; as completed records accumulate, the index doesn't grow; aligned precisely with the queries that matter
- **Expression index enables computed predicates** — `CREATE INDEX ON users(LOWER(email))` is required for `WHERE LOWER(email) = ?`; a plain `email` index cannot satisfy a case-insensitive lookup

PostgreSQL's index type selection starts with B-tree — it handles equality, ranges, and ORDER BY for the vast majority of queries. GIN and GiST exist for the cases B-tree can't handle: multi-value types and geometric data.

**B-tree — sorted, versatile, the default**
- B-tree keeps values in sorted order, which means it handles `=`, `>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'prefix%'`, and `ORDER BY` all from one structure; it's the index you get with `CREATE INDEX` without specifying a type
- Composite B-tree indexes follow the left-prefix rule — an index on `(user_id, status)` serves `WHERE user_id = ?` or both columns, but not `WHERE status = ?` alone

**GIN — for multi-value types**
- GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes every element inside a composite value — which means `WHERE data @> '{"role": "admin"}'` on a JSONB column uses a GIN index to find documents containing that key-value pair without scanning every row
- GIN also powers full-text search: `CREATE INDEX ON articles USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', body))` lets `WHERE body_search @@ to_tsquery('spring & boot')` use an index
- GIN is built once and is slower to update than B-tree, but extremely fast for containment queries on arrays, JSONB, and tsvector

**GiST — for geometric and range types**
- GiST (Generalized Search Tree) supports overlap, containment, and nearest-neighbor queries on geometric data types and range types
- `CREATE INDEX ON locations USING GIST(coordinates)` supports `WHERE coordinates && BOX(...)` — finding all points within a bounding box — which B-tree can't express

**Partial and expression indexes**
- A partial index with a WHERE clause indexes only matching rows: `CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'` — smaller, faster to maintain, precisely aligned with the query
- An expression index on `LOWER(email)` enables case-insensitive equality lookups without a full scan

questions.question: What are PostgreSQL transaction isolation levels? Explain the anomalies they prevent.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Transaction Isolation Levels
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL supports Read Committed (default), Repeatable Read, and Serializable. Each prevents different concurrency anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. PostgreSQL implements these via MVCC — readers never block writers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of MVCC and why Read Committed is safe for most queries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Serializable for all transactions — it has significant overhead and retry logic is required
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) as PostgreSQL's mechanism for isolation, and why readers never block

sections.content: Concurrency anomalies occur when multiple transactions run simultaneously. Higher isolation prevents more anomalies but reduces concurrency. PostgreSQL's MVCC means reads always see a consistent snapshot — no reader blocks a writer, no writer blocks a reader.

| Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read Committed (default) | ✅ Prevented | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible |
| Repeatable Read | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented* | ❌ Possible |
| Serializable | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented |

*PostgreSQL Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads (exceeds SQL standard requirement)

**Anomaly definitions:**
- **Dirty Read**: Read uncommitted data from another transaction (would roll back)
- **Non-Repeatable Read**: Re-reading a row gives different result (another transaction committed)
- **Phantom Read**: Re-running a query finds new rows (another transaction inserted)
- **Serialization Anomaly**: Result only possible if transactions didn't run concurrently

- **PostgreSQL MVCC: readers never block writers** — each row version is visible to the transactions that should see it; reads take a snapshot instead of acquiring shared locks
- **Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL also prevents phantom reads** — the MVCC snapshot taken at transaction start excludes rows inserted after; MySQL Repeatable Read requires gap locks and still has edge cases
- **Serializable uses SSI, not lock-based** — PostgreSQL detects dangerous read-write dependency cycles and aborts one transaction; lower contention than traditional lock-based Serializable isolation
- **Write skew requires Serializable** — two transactions each read shared state, make valid changes, and both commit — producing a state no serial execution could reach; only Serializable prevents this
- **Long transactions cause VACUUM bloat** — MVCC keeps old row versions alive while any transaction might need them; a long-running transaction blocks VACUUM from reclaiming dead rows, causing table bloat

PostgreSQL implements isolation levels through MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control. Every row has a version; when a transaction reads a row that another transaction is modifying, it sees the older version rather than blocking. This is why readers never block writers in PostgreSQL.

**Read Committed — the PostgreSQL default**
- Each statement in a transaction sees a fresh snapshot of committed data — which means two reads of the same row within one transaction may return different values if another transaction commits between them (non-repeatable read)
- This is the right default for most OLTP workloads and eliminates the need for shared locks on reads; most applications run correctly under Read Committed

**Repeatable Read — consistent snapshot from transaction start**
- PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read takes a snapshot at transaction start and holds it for all reads — which means the same row always returns the same value within one transaction, even if other transactions commit changes in between
- Unlike MySQL, PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads via MVCC — no gap locks needed because the snapshot simply doesn't show rows inserted after the snapshot was taken

**Serializable — prevents write skew**
- Serializable is the only level that prevents write skew — the anomaly where two transactions read overlapping data, make independent decisions, and both commit, leaving the database in a state no serial execution could produce
- PostgreSQL implements Serializable using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — it detects dangerous read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction rather than using traditional pessimistic locks; lower contention than lock-based Serializable

**MVCC trade-off: table bloat**
- Old row versions are kept until no active transaction needs them — which means long-running transactions prevent VACUUM from reclaiming space, causing table and index bloat; this is the most common PostgreSQL operational problem related to isolation

questions.question: How do you work with JSONB in PostgreSQL? When should you use JSONB vs relational columns?
questions.title: PostgreSQL JSONB — Queries, Indexing, and When to Use It
questions.direct_answer: JSONB stores JSON as binary for fast querying and indexing. Use JSONB for semi-structured or schema-flexible attributes (product metadata, user preferences). Use relational columns for data you filter, join, or aggregate frequently — indexes on JSONB are less efficient than on typed columns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical JSONB query knowledge and understanding of trade-offs vs relational design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using JSONB for everything ('document database in PostgreSQL') — loses all relational benefits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the @> containment operator and jsonb_each() for iterating keys, and when GIN vs B-Tree indexes apply

sections.content: JSONB stores JSON in a binary decomposed format — keys are sorted, types are preserved, and duplicate keys are removed. It supports operators for containment, key existence, and path traversal. GIN indexes make JSONB queries fast.

-- JSONB column definition:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    price       NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,   -- typed column for aggregation
    category    TEXT NOT NULL,             -- typed for joins
    attributes  JSONB                      -- semi-structured metadata
);

-- Sample data:
INSERT INTO products VALUES
(1, 'Widget Pro', 29.99, 'electronics',
 '{"color": "red", "weight_kg": 0.5, "tags": ["sale", "new"]}');

-- JSONB OPERATORS:
-- -> returns JSON:  attributes -> 'color' → '"red"'
-- ->> returns text: attributes ->> 'color' → 'red'
-- @> containment:   attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'
-- ? key exists:     attributes ? 'weight_kg'
-- #> path:          attributes #> '{specs,cpu}'

-- Query by JSONB attribute:
SELECT name, attributes ->> 'color' AS color
FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'   -- uses GIN index!
  AND attributes ? 'weight_kg';           -- key exists

-- Expand JSONB to rows:
SELECT name, key, value
FROM products,
     jsonb_each_text(attributes) AS kv(key, value)
WHERE category = 'electronics';

-- Update a specific JSONB key:
UPDATE products
SET attributes = jsonb_set(attributes, '{color}', '"blue"')
WHERE id = 1;

-- GIN index for containment queries:
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs_gin
    ON products USING GIN (attributes);
-- Now @> and ? operators use the index

sections.title: JSONB Query Patterns and Indexing Strategies
sections.content:
JSONB's power comes from its operator-based query language and GIN indexing. Knowing which operators are index-supported prevents full-table scans on JSONB columns.

**Containment operator (@>) for equality queries.** The `@>` operator checks if the left JSONB value contains the right value. This is the most GIN-index-friendly operator: `WHERE metadata @> '{"status": "active"}'` uses a GIN index efficiently. Use it instead of `->>`  comparison when checking for exact key-value matches.

**Path operators for nested access.** Use `->` to access a JSON object key and get a JSONB result. Use `->>` to get a text result. Use `#>` and `#>>` for nested path access: `metadata #>> '{address,city}'` extracts a deeply nested value. For WHERE clauses, prefer `@>` containment when possible because it uses GIN indexes; `->>`  text extraction requires a separate expression index.

```sql
-- GIN index covers containment queries
CREATE INDEX idx_products_metadata ON products USING GIN (metadata);

-- Efficient: uses GIN index
SELECT * FROM products WHERE metadata @> '{"brand": "Acme"}';

-- Inefficient: GIN index does NOT cover ->> extraction
SELECT * FROM products WHERE metadata ->> 'brand' = 'Acme';

-- Fix: create an expression index for ->> queries
CREATE INDEX idx_products_brand ON products ((metadata ->> 'brand'));
```

**When to extract JSONB fields into relational columns.** If you query or aggregate on a JSONB field frequently (e.g., filtering products by `metadata->>'brand'` in every listing page), extract it into a proper relational column with a regular B-tree index. JSONB is ideal for semi-structured data that varies between rows (custom attributes, user preferences, integration payloads). It is a poor choice for data you filter, sort, or join on regularly — relational columns with proper types and indexes outperform JSONB for these access patterns.

**JSONB in Spring Data JPA.** Use Hibernate's `@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)` annotation (Hibernate 6+) to map a Java object to a JSONB column. Spring Data's `@Query` with `nativeQuery = true` is required for JSONB operators because JPQL has no JSONB support. Alternatively, use the Specification pattern with a native SQL fragment for dynamic JSONB filters.

- **`jsonb` over `json` always** — `json` re-parses text on every read; `jsonb` stores binary, supports GIN indexing, and returns field extractions fast
- **GIN index enables `@>` containment queries** — `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN(data)` lets `WHERE data @> '{"status": "active"}'` avoid a full table scan
- **Expression index for specific-key equality** — `CREATE INDEX ON t ((data->>'email'))` enables `WHERE data->>'email' = ?` to use an index; a plain GIN index won't help equality on one extracted field
- **`->>` returns text; `->` returns JSON** — chain `->` for nested navigation, use `->>` at the final step for text comparison in WHERE; `WHERE data->>'count' = '5'` (text) not `= 5` (integer) unless you cast
- **Use JSONB for sparse or schema-flexible attributes** — product metadata, feature flags, and multi-tenant configuration benefit from JSONB; core relational attributes that appear on every row belong in typed columns with B-tree indexes

PostgreSQL's JSONB type stores JSON as binary and supports rich query operations with GIN indexing — making it possible to query semi-structured data at near-relational speed without leaving the relational database.

**JSONB vs JSON**
- `json` stores the raw text verbatim and re-parses it on every access — which means querying `json` columns is slower because the parsing happens each time
- `jsonb` stores JSON as parsed binary, which means field lookups are fast and the column can be GIN-indexed; this is the right choice for any JSON column you'll query

**Key operators**
- `->>` extracts a field as text: `data->>'status'` returns the status value as a string — used in WHERE clauses for equality filters
- `->` extracts a field as a JSON value: `data->'address'->>'city'` drills into nested objects
- `@>` checks containment: `WHERE data @> '{"role": "admin"}'` — returns documents where the JSON contains that key-value pair; this is the operator that uses a GIN index

**GIN indexing for fast containment queries**
- `CREATE INDEX ON users USING GIN(data)` — GIN indexes every key-value pair in the JSONB column, which means `WHERE data @> '{"role": "admin"}'` uses the index instead of scanning every row
- For equality on a specific key: `CREATE INDEX ON users ((data->>'email'))` — an expression index on the extracted field, used by `WHERE data->>'email' = ?`

**When to use JSONB vs normalized columns**
- Use JSONB for schema-flexible or sparse attributes — product metadata, feature flags, user preferences where different records legitimately have different fields
- Use normalized columns for core, always-present attributes that you filter, sort, or join on frequently — those benefit from typed columns with direct B-tree indexes

questions.question: Why do you need connection pooling for PostgreSQL? Compare PgBouncer modes.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Connection Pooling with PgBouncer
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL forks a process per connection — thousands of connections exhaust memory and hurt performance. PgBouncer pools connections, routing application connections to a smaller set of PostgreSQL server connections. Transaction mode is optimal for most Spring Boot applications.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of PostgreSQL's connection cost model and pooling trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Session mode in PgBouncer with connection limits — same as no pooling for high-concurrency apps
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the HikariCP (application-side) + PgBouncer (server-side) two-tier pooling pattern and why both are needed at scale

sections.content: PostgreSQL spawns a backend process per connection (not a thread). Each process uses ~5MB RAM. 1000 connections = 5GB just for idle connection overhead. PgBouncer sits between application and PostgreSQL, multiplexing many application connections to few server connections.

-- PostgreSQL connection cost:
-- SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity; → see current connections
-- SHOW max_connections; → default 100 (too low for microservices!)

-- Without pooling: 10 microservice instances × 10 HikariCP connections = 100 connections
-- Add Kubernetes scaling to 50 instances: 500 connections → PostgreSQL refuses!

-- PgBouncer pooling modes:
-- 1. SESSION mode: one server connection per client session
--    Client connects → gets dedicated PG connection for entire session
--    No benefit for stateless HTTP services!

-- 2. TRANSACTION mode (recommended for Spring Boot):
--    Client gets a PG connection only during a transaction
--    100 app connections, only 20 PG connections needed (80% idle time)

-- 3. STATEMENT mode:
--    Connection released after each statement
--    CANNOT use transactions, prepared statements
--    Rarely used

-- PgBouncer config:
-- pgbouncer.ini:
-- [databases]
-- mydb = host=postgres port=5432 dbname=mydb
-- [pgbouncer]
-- pool_mode = transaction          ← CRITICAL SETTING
-- max_client_conn = 1000           ← app connections
-- default_pool_size = 20           ← pg connections per database
-- server_pool_size = 5             ← max additional server connections

// Spring Boot datasource pointing to PgBouncer:
// spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://pgbouncer:6432/mydb
// spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=50  ← connects to PgBouncer
// PgBouncer maps these 50 to 20 PG server connections

- **PostgreSQL forks a process per connection** — not a thread; 500 connections = 500 OS processes; each idle connection consumes ~5-10MB RAM plus a backend process slot
- **PgBouncer transaction pooling: many clients, few PostgreSQL connections** — a single PostgreSQL connection handles many application requests serially; 10 real connections can serve 1,000 concurrent clients without 1,000 PostgreSQL processes
- **Transaction pooling vs session pooling** — transaction mode is most efficient (connection held only during the transaction); session mode holds it for the client session; statement mode is incompatible with multi-statement transactions
- **Prepared statements require configuration with PgBouncer** — transaction pooling mode breaks server-side prepared statements; set `prepareThreshold=0` in HikariCP or use `DISCARD ALL` after each connection return
- **HikariCP + PgBouncer as two layers** — HikariCP manages app-to-PgBouncer connections; PgBouncer manages PgBouncer-to-PostgreSQL connections; monitor both pool wait times independently

PostgreSQL creates a separate OS process per connection — not a thread, a full process. That means each idle connection consumes memory and a backend process slot even when it's doing nothing, which is the fundamental reason connection pooling is mandatory at scale.

**Why PostgreSQL needs external pooling**
- At 500 concurrent connections, PostgreSQL is running 500 backend processes — each consuming roughly 5-10MB of RAM just for the process overhead, before any query is executed
- Most web applications open far more connections than they need — a Spring Boot app with 50 threads per instance and 10 instances creates 500 connections at startup, most of them idle
- PgBouncer sits between the application and PostgreSQL, maintaining a small pool of real PostgreSQL connections while accepting many more from the application side

**PgBouncer pooling modes**
- Transaction pooling is the most efficient — the PostgreSQL connection is only held for the duration of a transaction, then returned to the pool; a single PostgreSQL connection can serve many application requests serially, which means 10 PostgreSQL connections can serve 1,000 concurrent application connections
- Session pooling holds the connection for the full client session — semantically identical to a direct connection; useful for compatibility but provides less multiplexing benefit
- Statement pooling holds the connection for a single statement — most efficient but incompatible with transactions and prepared statements; rarely used

**HikariCP + PgBouncer together**
- HikariCP manages the application-side connection pool to PgBouncer; PgBouncer manages the PostgreSQL-side pool — the two layers reduce connection count at both the application and database levels
- With transaction pooling, disable prepared statements at the PgBouncer level or configure HikariCP to use simple statements: `spring.datasource.hikari.data-source-properties.prepareThreshold=0`

questions.title: PostgreSQL Locking — Row Locks, Advisory Locks, Deadlock Prevention
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL uses row-level locks for DML and table-level locks for DDL. SELECT FOR UPDATE acquires row locks for consistent reads-for-update. Deadlocks occur when transactions lock rows in different orders. Prevent with consistent ordering; PostgreSQL auto-detects and aborts one transaction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of explicit locking for optimistic/pessimistic concurrency control
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that SELECT FOR UPDATE holds locks until transaction end — can cause significant contention
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain advisory locks for application-level distributed locking and the SKIP LOCKED pattern for work queues

sections.content:
- **MVCC: readers never block writers** — SELECT does not acquire row locks; updates to a row create a new version while readers continue reading the old version; eliminates reader-writer contention
- **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` acquires exclusive row locks** — prevents any concurrent UPDATE on those rows until the transaction commits; use for read-then-modify patterns like balance checks
- **Deadlock from inconsistent row lock order** — transactions that update rows in different orders deadlock; fix by enforcing consistent update order (by primary key) across all code paths
- **`lock_timeout` prevents indefinite blocking** — `SET lock_timeout = '5s'` in the session; a query waiting longer than 5s fails immediately rather than hanging; prevents cascading queue buildup
- **DDL acquires ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — use CONCURRENTLY** — `ALTER TABLE` blocks all reads and writes; `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` builds the index without blocking; `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT NULL` is instantaneous; non-null defaults require a table rewrite

Consider a real-world scenario: an e-commerce application has intermittent `ERROR: deadlock detected` errors in production. Two concurrent checkout processes both need to update inventory for the same products, but they process them in different orders based on the cart contents. Transaction 1 updates product A then B; Transaction 2 updates B then A. When both run simultaneously, each holds one lock and waits for the other — a classic **circular wait** deadlock.

**Detect lock waits in production:**
```sql
-- Show current lock waits:
SELECT
    blocking.pid AS blocking_pid,
    blocked.pid AS blocked_pid,
    blocking_activity.query AS blocking_query,
    blocked_activity.query AS blocked_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking_activity
    ON blocking_activity.pid = blocked.wait_event
WHERE blocked.wait_event IS NOT NULL;

-- See lock details:
SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted;

-- Log deadlocks automatically:
-- postgresql.conf: deadlock_timeout = 1s  (check for deadlock after 1s)
-- log_lock_waits = on  (log waits > deadlock_timeout)
```

The fix is to ensure all transactions lock rows in the **same deterministic order**. Here are three approaches, from simplest to most powerful:

**Fix 1: Sort IDs before locking** — the application sorts the product IDs so every transaction acquires locks in alphabetical/numerical order:

```sql
-- Both Tx1 and Tx2 now lock in the SAME order: A first, then B
-- This makes circular waits structurally impossible
BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM inventory
  WHERE product_id IN ('A', 'B')
  ORDER BY product_id   -- ← consistent ordering = no deadlocks
  FOR UPDATE;           -- ← locks acquired in sorted order
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1
  WHERE product_id IN ('A', 'B');
COMMIT;
```

**Fix 2: In Spring Data JPA**, sort the IDs in Java before passing them to the query:

```java
// Sort product IDs in the service layer before the repository call
Collections.sort(productIds);
inventoryRepository.decrementAll(productIds);

// Repository — ORDER BY ensures lock acquisition order matches
@Modifying
@Query("UPDATE Inventory i SET i.quantity = i.quantity - 1 "
     + "WHERE i.productId IN :ids ORDER BY i.productId")
void decrementAll(@Param("ids") List<String> sortedIds);
```

**Bonus: SKIP LOCKED** — PostgreSQL's built-in work queue pattern, perfect for background job processing without an external message broker:

```sql
-- Each worker grabs the next UNLOCKED pending job
-- If another worker already locked a row, SKIP LOCKED skips it silently
SELECT * FROM job_queue
  WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  ORDER BY created_at     -- oldest job first
  LIMIT 1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; -- skip rows locked by other workers
-- No blocking, no deadlocks, no RabbitMQ needed for simple cases
```

**Advisory locks** — lightweight application-level locks for cross-instance coordination:

```sql
-- Returns true if lock acquired, false if another session holds it
-- Lock ID is any bigint — use a hash of your job name
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('nightly-report'));
-- Lock auto-releases when transaction ends
-- Use case: ensure only one app instance runs the nightly report
```

PostgreSQL locking has one significant advantage over most other databases: MVCC means readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Locks in PostgreSQL primarily come from explicit write operations, not from reads.

**Row-level locks — how DML acquires them**
- `UPDATE` and `DELETE` acquire a row-level exclusive lock on the rows they modify — other transactions that try to UPDATE or DELETE the same rows wait until the first transaction commits or rolls back
- `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` explicitly acquires a row lock for the current transaction — useful when you need to read a row and guarantee no one else updates it before you do, like the pattern "read balance, check if sufficient, deduct"
- `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` acquires a shared row lock — allows concurrent reads but blocks updates; use when you want to prevent modification but allow other readers

**Deadlocks — how they happen and how to avoid them**
- Deadlock occurs when transaction A holds a lock that transaction B wants, and B holds a lock that A wants — both block indefinitely; PostgreSQL detects this cycle and aborts one transaction with a deadlock error
- The most common cause is inconsistent update order — transaction A updates rows in order (1, 2, 3) while transaction B updates them in order (3, 2, 1); the fix is always updating rows in consistent primary key order across all code paths
- Lock timeouts prevent indefinite blocking: `SET lock_timeout = '5s'` in the session causes a query to fail rather than wait more than 5 seconds for a lock

**Table-level locks from DDL**
- `ALTER TABLE` acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which blocks all reads and writes on the table during the operation — for large tables, use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` with nullable defaults to avoid blocking
- `pg_locks` shows currently held locks; `pg_blocking_pids()` identifies which session is blocking another

questions.question: How does table partitioning work in PostgreSQL? When should you partition a table?
questions.title: PostgreSQL Table Partitioning — Range, List, and Hash
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL declarative partitioning splits a large table into physical child tables based on a partition key. Range partitioning by date enables partition pruning — queries with date filters only scan relevant partitions. Use when tables exceed 50-100M rows or old data is regularly archived.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of partitioning as a scaling strategy for large time-series tables
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Partitioning small tables — it adds overhead without benefit; benefits only emerge at very large scale
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain partition pruning and why the partition key must be included in queries for pruning to work

sections.content: Partitioning physically splits a large table into smaller child tables. The parent table is a virtual routing layer — queries go to the parent and PostgreSQL routes them to relevant partitions. The key benefit is partition pruning: if your query filters by the partition key, PostgreSQL only scans matching partitions.

-- RANGE PARTITIONING by month (most common for time-series)
CREATE TABLE events (
    id          BIGSERIAL,
    user_id     BIGINT,
    event_type  TEXT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    payload     JSONB
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- Create monthly partitions:
CREATE TABLE events_2026_01
    PARTITION OF events
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-02-01');

CREATE TABLE events_2026_02
    PARTITION OF events
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-02-01') TO ('2026-03-01');

-- Indexes are created per partition:
CREATE INDEX ON events_2026_01 (user_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ON events_2026_02 (user_id, created_at DESC);

-- Query with partition key → partition pruning:
EXPLAIN
SELECT * FROM events
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-02-01' AND '2026-03-01'
  AND user_id = 42;
-- → Only scans events_2026_02, not all other partitions!

-- Query WITHOUT partition key → full scan of all partitions:
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 42;
-- → Scans ALL partitions — doesn't benefit from partitioning!

-- Archive old data (instant! Just detach partition):
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2025_01;
-- events_2025_01 now standalone table, can be moved to cold storage

-- Automate with pg_partman extension:
-- Creates, maintains, and drops partitions automatically

- **Partition pruning requires the partition key in WHERE** — a query without the partition column scans all partitions; partition-key-less queries are slower than the equivalent non-partitioned query
- **RANGE partitioning on timestamp columns is the most useful pattern** — monthly or yearly partitions with date-bounded queries prune naturally; archiving drops an entire partition in milliseconds
- **`DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY`** — removes a partition from the parent table without locking it; the detached partition becomes a standalone table for archiving without blocking ongoing queries
- **Unique constraints must include the partition key** — PostgreSQL cannot enforce uniqueness across partition boundaries without the partition key in the constraint; design primary keys accordingly
- **Indexes must be created on child partitions** — a `CREATE INDEX` on the parent creates indexes on all current and future partitions automatically (PostgreSQL 11+); verify with `\d+ tablename` in psql

PostgreSQL declarative partitioning splits a large table into physical child tables while presenting them as a single logical table. It's most useful for time-series data where queries are naturally bounded by a date range.

**How partition pruning works**
- When a query includes the partition key in WHERE, the planner eliminates partitions that cannot contain matching rows — `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'` scans only the January partition instead of every partition in the table
- Without the partition key in WHERE, all partitions are scanned — which is often slower than a non-partitioned table due to per-partition planning overhead; partition pruning is the only reason to partition

**Declaring partitions**
- `PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)` defines the partitioning strategy on the parent; each child partition is declared with `CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01 PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01')`
- List partitioning (`PARTITION BY LIST (region)`) works for discrete values — partitioning by tenant or region when queries are always scoped to one value
- Hash partitioning distributes rows evenly — useful for write distribution, but provides no pruning benefit for selective reads

**Archiving — the operational win**
- `DETACH PARTITION orders_2022_01 CONCURRENTLY` removes a partition from the table without locking the parent — the detached partition becomes a standalone table that can be archived or dropped
- `DROP TABLE orders_2022_01` then removes the data instantly, rather than running a DELETE that generates per-row WAL records for millions of rows

**What partitioning doesn't fix**
- Cross-partition queries that don't prune are slower than unpartitioned tables — the planner must account for all partitions in the query plan
- Unique constraints must include the partition key; foreign keys referencing a partitioned table require the partition key in the FK

questions.question: How do you solve the N+1 query problem in Spring Data JPA with PostgreSQL?
questions.title: N+1 Query Problem — Detection and Solutions with JPA + PostgreSQL
questions.direct_answer: N+1 occurs when loading N entities triggers N additional queries for associated data. Fix with JOIN FETCH (JPQL), @EntityGraph (annotation), or batch fetching. Detect with Hibernate's SQL logging or the p6spy library.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical JPA performance knowledge for the most common ORM performance problem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using EAGER loading on @OneToMany to fix N+1 — this fetches all associations even when not needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Hibernate batch fetching strategy as an alternative to JOIN FETCH and when DTO projections are better than entities

sections.content: Loading 100 orders for a page generates 101 SQL queries: 1 to load orders, then 100 more to load each order's items via LAZY loading when the view renders. Page load time: 2.3 seconds instead of 200ms.

**Enable SQL logging to detect N+1:**
```yaml
spring.jpa.show-sql: true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql: true
logging.level.org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql: TRACE  # show parameters
```

Or use Hypersistence Utilities' `assertNoSQLStatements()` in tests:
```java
long queryCount = executionContext.getQueries().size();
assertThat(queryCount).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2); // should be 2 queries, not 101
```

- **N+1 = 1 query for the list + 1 query per entity for the association** — 100 orders with lazy items = 101 queries; `EXPLAIN` shows this as 101 separate index lookups instead of one JOIN
- **`JOIN FETCH` eliminates N+1 for single associations** — `SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items` returns orders and items in one query; limited to one collection per query before Cartesian products appear
- **`@EntityGraph` is the declarative alternative** — `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items"})` on a repository method generates a LEFT JOIN without modifying the JPQL; different graphs per method
- **`@BatchSize` for multiple collections** — `@BatchSize(size = 25)` batches association loading into IN-list queries; turns 100 selects into 4; avoids Cartesian products that JOIN FETCH creates for two collections
- **`spring.jpa.show-sql=true` catches N+1 in development** — count the SQL queries in the log for a single HTTP request; more than 5-10 queries for one request usually indicates N+1

The N+1 query problem is the most common JPA performance issue. It happens when loading N entities causes N additional queries for associated data — one SELECT for the list, then one SELECT per entity for a related collection.

**How it happens with Hibernate**
- Hibernate loads associations lazily by default — `order.getItems()` triggers a SELECT the first time the collection is accessed in the same transaction
- If you fetch 100 orders and access `.getItems()` on each in a loop, Hibernate executes 1 query for the orders plus 100 queries for the items — 101 queries total instead of 1 joined query

**Fetch join — fix for simple associations**
- `JOIN FETCH` in JPQL loads the association in the initial query: `SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items WHERE o.status = 'ACTIVE'` returns orders with their items in one database round trip
- The limitation: you can only JOIN FETCH one collection per query without getting a Cartesian product; for two collections, use `@EntityGraph` with separate fetching strategies or batch fetching

**@EntityGraph — declarative eager loading**
- `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items", "customer"})` on a repository method tells Hibernate to load those associations with the query instead of lazily — generating a LEFT JOIN in the SQL without modifying the JPQL
- Cleaner than adding FETCH to JPQL for simple cases; allows different fetching strategies per repository method

**Batch fetching — for collections**
- `@BatchSize(size = 25)` on a collection field tells Hibernate to load up to 25 collections in one IN-list query instead of N individual queries — turns 100 queries into 4, without requiring a JOIN FETCH
- This is the best option when JOIN FETCH would cause a Cartesian product (fetching two or more collections on the same entity)

Always enable SQL logging in development to catch N+1 before production: `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` and `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG`.

questions.question: How do you implement full-text search in PostgreSQL?
questions.title: Full-Text Search in PostgreSQL — tsvector, tsquery, and GIN
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL has native full-text search via tsvector (document representation) and tsquery (search query). Create a GIN index on to_tsvector for fast search. For simple use cases, this eliminates the need for Elasticsearch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of PostgreSQL's built-in FTS as an alternative to external search engines
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using LIKE '%keyword%' for search (can't use index, slow on large tables)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain lexemes, stemming, and ranking with ts_rank, and when Elasticsearch is still needed (facets, relevance tuning, distributed scale)

sections.content: PostgreSQL's full-text search converts text to lexemes (normalized word forms), removes stop words, and enables efficient search via GIN index. It supports stemming, phrase search, boolean operators, and relevance ranking — without an external service.

sections.title: Step 1: Create a tsvector column with GIN index
sections.content:
```sql
-- Option A: Generated column (auto-updated)
ALTER TABLE articles
    ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        to_tsvector('english',
            coalesce(title, '') || ' ' ||
            coalesce(body, ''))
    ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX idx_articles_fts
    ON articles USING GIN (search_vector);

-- Option B: Expression index (no extra column)
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_fts
    ON articles USING GIN (
        to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || body)
    );
```

sections.title: Step 2: Query with tsquery
sections.content:
```sql
-- Basic search:
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'postgresql & indexing');
-- Finds articles containing both 'postgresql' AND 'indexing' (stemmed!)
-- 'indexing' matches 'index', 'indexed', 'indexes'

-- plainto_tsquery: user-friendly (no need for & | operators)
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'postgres full text search');
-- Automatically adds AND between words

-- phraseto_tsquery: exact phrase
WHERE search_vector @@ phraseto_tsquery('english', 'full text search');
-- Words must appear in sequence

-- Ranking results by relevance:
SELECT id, title,
    ts_rank(search_vector, query) AS rank
FROM articles,
     to_tsquery('english', 'postgresql') query
WHERE search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Highlight matched terms:
SELECT id,
    ts_headline('english', body,
        to_tsquery('postgresql'),
        'MaxWords=50, MinWords=25') AS snippet
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('postgresql');
```

sections.title: Step 3: Spring Data JPA integration

sections.content:
- **`tsvector` stores the processed document; `tsquery` expresses the search** — `@@` matches them; GIN index on the tsvector makes search sub-second instead of a full table scan
- **Stemming and stop-word removal are automatic** — `to_tsvector('english', body)` strips "the", "is", and normalizes "running" to "run"; search results match morphological variants without the caller managing it
- **GIN index is required for performance** — `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', body))`; without it, every search recomputes tsvector for every row and scans the full table
- **`ts_rank` provides relevance scoring** — orders results by term frequency and position; supports covering queries where some terms matter more than others with weight vectors
- **PostgreSQL FTS is sufficient for simple search; Elasticsearch for complex cases** — faceted navigation, autocomplete, fuzzy matching, and datasets of 100M+ documents benefit from Elasticsearch; adding it for basic keyword search on a small dataset adds operational complexity without proportional benefit

PostgreSQL has native full-text search built around two types: `tsvector` (a processed document representation) and `tsquery` (a search query). For many applications, this is sufficient without adding Elasticsearch.

**How it works**
- `to_tsvector('english', body)` processes text through PostgreSQL's built-in text analyzer — it tokenizes words, strips stop words (the, a, is), and applies stemming so "running" and "runs" match the same term
- `to_tsquery('english', 'spring & boot')` parses the search query into stemmed terms with boolean operators; `@@` is the match operator — `WHERE body_tsvector @@ query` returns documents containing both terms

**Indexing for performance**
- Store the tsvector in a generated column or pre-computed column and index it: `CREATE INDEX ON articles USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', body))` — GIN is the only index type that supports full-text search
- Without the GIN index, `to_tsvector` is computed on every row for every query — a full table scan for every search; the GIN index makes searches sub-second on millions of documents

**Ranking results**
- `ts_rank(tsvector, tsquery)` returns a relevance score — `ORDER BY ts_rank(body_tsvector, query) DESC` ranks results by how frequently and prominently the search terms appear
- `ts_headline` generates highlighted snippets showing the search terms in context — useful for displaying matched excerpts in search results

**PostgreSQL FTS vs Elasticsearch**
- PostgreSQL FTS is sufficient for: simple keyword search on one or two columns, existing PostgreSQL databases where adding Elasticsearch adds operational overhead, searches on small-to-medium datasets (up to a few million documents)
- Elasticsearch is the better choice for: complex relevance tuning, faceted search, autocomplete, fuzzy matching, cross-field search, or datasets of hundreds of millions of documents

items: tsvector stores the processed document; tsquery expresses the search — @@ matches them; GIN index on the tsvector makes search sub-second instead of a full table scan Stemming and stop-word removal are automatic — to_tsvector('english', body) strips "the", "is", and normalizes "running" to "run"; search results match morphological variants without the caller managing it GIN index is required for performance — CREATE INDEX

USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', body)); without it, every search recomputes tsvector for every row and scans the full table ts_rank provides relevance scoring — orders results by term frequency and position; supports covering queries where some terms matter more than others with weight vectors PostgreSQL FTS is sufficient for simple search; Elasticsearch for complex cases — faceted navigation, autocomplete, fuzzy matching, and datasets of 100M+ documents benefit from Elasticsearch; adding it for basic keyword search on a small dataset adds operational complexity without proportional benefit
